title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of one‑shot LLM intent→configuration generation and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes (study_id = rX4f7-1). Using the requested model gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation, we applied a preregistered binary episode success rule (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). Of 1,200 planned paired tasks we completed 1,199 pairs. Baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0000000000). The paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002502085070892446 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957], bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. The preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory hypothesis (H3) was not executed as a separate confirmatory test and therefore is not part of the reported inferential results; the archived analysis contains only the pooled paired analysis artifacts (see Methods and Results for explicit artifact pointers). Representative validator traces and provider audit logs show repair was invoked only three times. Under these controlled emulation and task‑corpus conditions we find no statistically significant advantage for the verifier‑assisted pipeline; we report artifacts, analytic deviation (Wilcoxon → exact McNemar for binary outcomes), and execution accounting to support reproducible interpretation.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent expressed in natural language into executable device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Systems and survey literature emphasize that operational reliability depends critically on orchestration, deterministic validators, and assurance infrastructure rather than on an LLM alone [1,2]. Generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architectures are a canonical mitigation strategy: an LLM proposes candidate outputs, an automated verifier checks constraints and safety, and an automated repair loop iterates until the candidate satisfies verifier rules [3–5]. Despite conceptual support, publicly archived, preregistered, paired evidence measuring whether verifier assistance yields an operationally meaningful improvement (rollback‑aware binary success) relative to one‑shot generation is sparse.

We address this gap with NetOpsTraceBench: a preregistered, paired, emulator‑grounded study comparing (A) baseline one‑shot NL→config generation and (B) a guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline using the same shared initial candidate per pair. The preregistered design included three confirmatory hypotheses (H1–H3). H1 (primary) tested whether verifier assistance increases the paired binary success rate; H3 prespecified a topology‑cluster breakdown (edge vs core) as a confirmatory subgroup comparison. The execution produced a pooled paired confirmatory analysis (reported here); the preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory hypothesis H3 was not executed as a separate confirmatory test and therefore is not included in the inferential results. The Methods and Results below state this explicitly and point to the archived pooled analysis artifacts.
sections.related_work:
Recent survey and system literature frames LLMs as components inside broader AIOps/NetOps workflows and repeatedly emphasizes that correctness and trustworthiness are properties of the whole orchestration stack (model + verifier + provenance + sandboxed execution), not of the base LLM alone [1–3]. Multiple community reviews urge workflow‑centered evaluation—trace quality, validator interactions, and rollback‑aware metrics—rather than isolated one‑shot QA tests; these reviews motivate reproducible, audit‑ready benchmarks that combine generation, deterministic validation, and emulation [1,2,4].

Concrete verifier‑assisted approaches appear across adjacent domains and NetOps prototypes. Work on NL→formal translations and CTL/specification generation demonstrates generator+verifier loops where formal checks drive iterative repairs; topology‑compilation systems translate high‑level security intent into executable topologies with compliance checks and constraint enforcement [5,6]. Prototype efforts in the configuration space (text→config generators and misconfiguration detectors) and domain‑specific “LLM firewalls” illustrate practical patterns: an LLM proposes a candidate, an automated validator enforces syntactic and semantic constraints, and an orchestrator optionally triggers constrained repair or rejects the proposal [7–10].

Empirical and conceptual studies document LLM failure modes (hallucination, unit/semantic errors, overconfidence, provenance loss, prompt‑injection) that motivate guarded architectures and verifier scaffolding [11–14]. These works support the rationale for a workflow‑centered paired benchmark but also warn that measured gains depend on corpus difficulty and verifier configuration.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand: The study was preregistered as NetOpsTraceBench (study_id = rX4f7-1) and the preregistration manifest (SHA‑256 = 77abe8b493bde44484e0b3d02cfd7f9ec1621ff7e7847889082ae177a7ed5712) froze confirmatory hypotheses (H1–H3), inclusion/exclusion rules, seeds, stopping rules, analysis executor, and a prespecified power target (MDE = 5 percentage points). The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; the prespecified analysis executor is paired_binary_analysis_v1.

Task corpus and topology clusters: The benchmark scope defined 1,200 deterministic operator‑intent tasks split into two simulated topology clusters labeled edge (600) and core (600). Tasks were produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (generator_version = 5.0) with frozen generation_seed values and encoded required_sequence, initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_touched_fields, and declared difficulty metadata. Task provenance and contamination controls were incorporated in generation.

Paired pipeline semantics and shared_initial_candidate design choice: To isolate verifier and repair effects from initial generation variability we implemented a shared_initial_candidate protocol: for each task a single initial candidate configuration was generated and supplied to both baseline (one‑shot) and guarded (verifier‑assisted) episodes. This choice reduces variance attributable to independent generation and ensures the paired comparison measures the verifier/repair intervention rather than differing initial generations. The design decision is archived and reproducible in the execution artifacts (examples in execution/responses/* and execution/provider_calls/*), and it explains why repair invocation counts directly reflect verifier rejections of the same candidate rather than divergent LLM proposals.

Pipeline implementation, validator, and operational scoring: Adapter orchestration used hosted_netops_gvr_v1; model requests used the requested_model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json records requested_model=gpt-5-mini, max_output_tokens=1500). Per preregistration, initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; retrieval_augmented_generation = false; independent_condition_generation = false (shared initial candidate). The deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces canonical parsing, workflow_policies, required_command_count checks, and emits validation_before/validation_after diagnostics; the preregistered binary episode success requires (a) validation_after.valid == true, (b) emulator availability within tolerance, and (c) no automatic rollback event.

Contamination, exclusions, and stopping rule: Contamination thresholds (token/subsequence overlap T_contam = 0.85 and optional embedding cosine threshold 0.92) and exclusion rules were preregistered. The run halts only if model calls reach maximum_model_calls = 2,400 or deterministic components fail irrecoverably per frozen retry policy. Execution produced provider_call_audit entries (hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,202; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1). All seeds, code, validator rules, repair prompts, and provider traces are archived.

Confirmatory hypothesis H3 (topology‑cluster breakdown) status: H3 was preregistered as a confirmatory subgroup comparison across the two topology clusters. The archived confirmatory analysis executed and archived only the pooled paired binary analysis (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json). The preregistered cluster‑breakdown confirmatory test (H3) was not executed as a separate confirmatory inference and therefore is not reported as part of the confirmatory results. This manuscript corrects earlier language that implied a completed per‑cluster confirmatory inference by explicitly noting H3's non‑execution and pointing readers to the pooled analysis artifacts for reproduction.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and pair completion: The run completed 2,398 of 2,400 planned episodes and produced 1,199 complete paired observations (complete_pair_count = 1,199; failed_episode_count = 2). Provider audit records hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203 and stage_counts show shared_initial_generation = 1,200 and repair = 3, indicating a single shared initial generation per task and only three repair‑stage LLM calls across the corpus.

Primary pooled confirmatory outcomes (pooled across topology clusters): The paired 2×2 contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 1,196 (both succeeded), n10 = 3 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Baseline_success_rate = 1,196/1,199 = 0.9974979149291076; guarded_success_rate = 1,199/1,199 = 1.0. Observed paired‑success‑rate difference = 0.002502085070892446.

Inferential results and CI: Because outcomes are binary and concentrated in concordant cells, the archived confirmatory inference used an exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant counts (n10 = 3, n01 = 0): exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with bootstrap_seed = 1729 and bootstrap_resamples = 10,000 (archived in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and analysis/results.json) is [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957]. Both the p‑value and CI are reproduced exactly from archived analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json).

Missingness, exclusions, and contamination: analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 1,199; failed_baseline_episodes = 1; failed_guarded_episodes = 1; both_missing_pairs = 1. Contamination checks produced no exclusions (analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty).

Repair invocation diagnostics and representative artifacts: Stage_counts and scoring traces show repair = 3 and that most initial candidates were accepted by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validation_after.valid = true; repair_applied = false in representative scoring JSONs execution/scoring/*.json). Representative per‑task artifacts (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json, execution/responses/task-000001-*.txt, and task_manifest entries) illustrate shared_initial_candidate semantics, difficulty labels, normalized_configuration values, and validator diagnostics that underpin the pooled counts.

Topology‑cluster confirmatory hypothesis (H3) not executed: The preregistration's H3 planned a confirmatory paired breakdown by topology cluster (edge vs core). The archived confirmatory results include only the pooled paired test; no separate confirmatory per‑cluster contingency tables or p‑values were produced or archived. Readers can reproduce the pooled analysis from analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv; per‑cluster confirmatory inference was not executed and therefore is not reported here.
sections.discussion:
Statistical interpretation and headroom constraints: The pooled exact McNemar p = 0.25 and bootstrap CI that includes zero indicate no statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline under the preregistered pooled analysis. Two archived, artifact‑grounded explanations are supported. First, near‑ceiling baseline performance (≈99.75%) left minimal absolute headroom for improvement compared with the preregistered MDE (5 percentage points). The observed discordant counts (n10 = 3, n01 = 0) are too small to yield confirmatory significance for small absolute effects; the archived bootstrap CI and discordant counts quantify this limitation.

Second, shared_initial_candidate semantics and corpus/validator design materially affected repair invocation. The shared_initial_candidate design intentionally isolates verifier/repair effects—but it also means that when the deterministic task generator and validator produce well‑specified tasks and acceptance criteria, the initial LLM outputs often satisfy verifier checks and repair is seldom invoked (repair_stage_calls = 3). This interaction is visible in representative scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/*.json) and explains the low discordant count.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is strong due to deterministic seeds and automated exclusion rules; construct validity depends on whether the preregistered binary success rule maps to operationally meaningful correctness across production environments. External validity is limited: only the requested_model = gpt-5-mini was exercised, tasks were synthetic/consented and vendor‑agnostic, and Mininet‑style emulation may not capture vendor idiosyncrasies. Verifier configuration dependence is a major concern: different validator strictness would likely change repair rates and paired outcomes.

Implications and next steps: When initial generation already meets deterministic verifier criteria for well‑specified tasks, generate–validate–repair will be infrequently exercised and measured gains on a binary success metric will be small. To evaluate verifier value more thoroughly, future experiments should (a) increase task ambiguity/adversariality, (b) vary verifier strictness, (c) exercise multiple model families, and (d) perform the preregistered topology‑cluster breakdown as a confirmatory test when power and discordant counts permit. The archived artifacts provided with this run (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json, execution/execution_manifest.json, execution/scoring/*.json) enable reproducible sensitivity studies without new data collection.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired, emulator‑grounded study comparing one‑shot and verifier‑assisted NL→configuration pipelines on 1,199 completed pairs. Under our deterministic synthetic corpus, validator configuration, shared_initial_candidate pairing, and requested_model = gpt-5-mini, baseline one‑shot generation achieved near‑ceiling success (≈99.75%). The guarded pipeline increased absolute success by ≈0.25 percentage points; the pooled confirmatory exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25 and a 95% bootstrap CI include zero. The preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory hypothesis H3 was not executed as a separate confirmatory test and is therefore not claimed here; the pooled analysis artifacts are archived for reproduction. The run artifacts and analysis logs (artifact_count = 8,408) provide a reproducible basis for sensitivity and follow‑up studies that vary corpus difficulty, verifier strictness, and model family to determine conditions where verifier scaffolding yields operationally meaningful improvements.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, transient telemetry).

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary. This deviation is recorded in the archived analysis artifacts and in the Disclosure Statement above.

Confirmatory H3 not executed: the preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory hypothesis (H3) was not executed as a separate confirmatory test; the manuscript reports the pooled confirmatory analysis only and points to the archived pooled analysis artifacts for reproduction.
